headline: Peanut Bunker Push: Blues Crash Second Beach While Bass Go Nocturnal on the Ledges
subhead: Warm water has stripers hunting after dark off the rocks from Newport to Sakonnet, while bluefish tear up bait schools along the open beaches and the breachways wait on their first albie.
body_markdown:
Peanut bunker are stacked so thick against the rocks at Second Beach right now you can see the water nervous from fifty yards out — that flickering, silver shiver that tells you something's underneath pushing them. Same story along the wash at Matunuck and down at East Beach in Charlestown. That bait's been getting worked hard for about ten days, and it's the bluefish doing the damage, not the bass, which tells you a lot about where this water's sitting right now.

Surface temps have been running warm — mid-70s to pushing 80 in the shallow coves — and that's outside the comfort window stripers like. So the bass haven't left, they've just gone underground. I've been hopping the ledges below Fort Adams and out around Beavertail in Jamestown at first light and getting nothing but small stuff and a few short bass mixed with scup, but the same water at 9 PM with an eel or a chunk of bunker on a fish-finder rig fished tight to the rock face has been a different animal. Two nights last week I had fish to 34 inches off the ledges below Castle Hill, both on the last two hours of the outgoing with the current still moving good. Sakonnet Point's fishing the same way — daytime is quiet, but work the rip off the point after dark on a big bunker head or a whole eel drifted through the seam where the current splits around the rocks, and there are bass willing to eat. This is a warm-water pattern through and through: bass feeding on the tide changes and in the dark, holding deep and tight to structure through the heat of the day. Nothing wrong with the fish being there, you just have to fish the clock instead of the sun.

Bluefish are the ones cashing in on this warm stretch, and they're not shy about it. Second Beach has had gulls working bait pods just off the sandbar most mornings this week, and if you can get a Hopkins or a diamond jig out past the breakers before the blues push the bunker into the whitewash, it's a fish a cast for a stretch. Same read at Weekapaug and along the beach toward Napatree — peanut bunker and small mullet getting hammered right at the surf line, blues running 3 to 6 pounds with the occasional bigger one mixed in. Bring wire or heavy fluoro leader, because these fish are cutting people off left and right on straight mono.

Fluke have been the honest, dependable part of the week. Nothing explosive, but a steady bottom bite off Jamestown along the Dumplings and out toward Whale Rock, drifting 4-inch white Gulp swimming mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails in 25 to 35 feet of water on the last of the incoming into the top of the tide. Keepers mixed with a good number of shorts — I'd call it a two-keeper, six-fish kind of drift most days, which is fine for August. Sakonnet River channel edges near the Tap's have produced similarly, best on slack-adjacent water when the drift slows enough to keep the bait down.

Tog talk is quiet right now, and that's expected — this warm a stretch of water, they're tucked deep in the cracks and not feeding hard. I've marked good numbers of fish on the sounder around the rockpiles off Newport and out at Whale Rock, which tells me the population's there and waiting. That's a September conversation, not an August one. Worth remembering those spots now while the water's warm and easy to read, because when the first cold nights knock the temperature down, that's when the green crabs go back in the bucket and those same rocks turn on.

As for albies — we flagged the breachways as the spot to watch heading into this stretch, and the ingredients are still lining up but the fish haven't shown yet. Squid are building in numbers around the RI shoreline according to what's been reported to our east, which is exactly the kind of forage shift that pulls albies and bonito tight to structure once the water temperature and current pattern lock in. Napatree and the Watch Hill side of the breachway are where I'd keep half an eye out starting this week — small epoxy jigs and Deadly Dicks ready in the bag — but I wouldn't plan a trip around it yet. It's a scouting mission right now, not a sure thing.

Look at the week ahead and I don't see much reason for this pattern to break. Warm, stable water, no major weather disruption in sight, tide building back toward the mid-August new moon — that keeps bass on the night program, blues chewing the beaches during daylight, and fluke steady on the structure drifts. If I had one trip to make, I'd fish last light into full dark off the Jamestown or Sakonnet ledges on bunker or eel, and I'd carry a light spinning rod rigged for albies just in case that breachway bait gets nervous while I'm standing there. Won't cost you anything to be ready.
